title: Depreciation Methods
description: Calculate depreciation using straight-line, declining-balance and units-of-production methods.
html:
What is depreciation?

Depreciation systematically allocates the depreciable amount of a tangible long-lived asset over its useful life.

Depreciation is an allocation process. It does not simply attempt to measure the asset's change in market value.

Straight-Line Depreciation

Annual Depreciation = (Cost − Residual Value) ÷ Useful Life

Example

Equipment costs $50,000, has a $5,000 residual value, and a 5-year useful life.

($50,000 − $5,000) ÷ 5 = $9,000 per year

Carrying Amount

Carrying Amount = Asset Cost − Accumulated Depreciation

After two full years:

Asset Cost $50,000
Accumulated Depreciation ($18,000)
Carrying Amount $32,000

Units-of-Production

This method bases depreciation on actual usage or production rather than simply the passage of time.

Depreciation Per Unit = (Cost − Residual Value) ÷ Estimated Total Units

Declining-Balance Methods

Accelerated methods recognize more depreciation in earlier years and less in later years.

Double-Declining Balance

For a 5-year asset, the straight-line rate is 20%. A double-declining rate would therefore be 40%.

The rate is applied to the asset's beginning carrying amount each year.

Remember

  • Straight-line → equal depreciation each full year
  • Units-of-production → based on usage
  • Accelerated methods → more depreciation earlier

quiz.prompt: Equipment costs $100,000, has a $10,000 residual value and a 6-year useful life. What is annual straight-line depreciation?
